item.title: Does your probiotic drink actually stay in your gut?
item.description: Probiotics may not colonize your gut. Studies show that probiotics did not markedly alter the core gut microbiome or detectably colonize the gut environment of arctic char after a 4-week treatment. The evidence shows that probiotic effects are highly variable, with some studies showing significant impacts on infant microbiomes while others show no detectable colonization or core microbiome alteration in fish.

item.title: Do you choose your actions, or do they happen to you?
item.description: Neural signals before your choice are not the cause of it. Research shows that the readiness potential is unrelated to your conscious intentions and does not cause you to act. The evidence shows that the readiness potential is not a reliable indicator of conscious will or the causal mechanism for it.

item.title: Is your social capital actually disappearing?
item.description: Remote work shows no evidence of eroding weak ties. While telecommuting is linked to work overload in secret places and an eroded line between personal and professional life, there is no data showing it harms long-term innovation or organizational social capital. The provided sources do not contain data regarding the erosion of organizational social capital or 'weak ties' due to remote work.

item.title: Is your healthy snack linked to mortality?
item.description: Ultra-processed food is linked to higher mortality. High consumption of ultra-processed foods is linked to an increased risk of all-cause mortality. The evidence consistently links high consumption of ultra-processed foods to a wide range of adverse health outcomes including mortality, cardiovascular disease, and mental health disorders.

item.title: Does your routine leave a physical mark on your brain?
item.description: Your brain changes based on your actions. Significant changes in brain activation, structure, and connectivity are reported in the majority of studies involving different types of training. The provided sources do not contain any information regarding smartphones or social media, making it impossible to support the proposed angle.

item.title: Can bacteria learn to survive every medicine?
item.description: Bacteria evolve resistance in nearly every lineage. When exposed to specific antimicrobial peptides, 22 out of 24 lineages of Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas fluorescens independently developed heritable resistance. The evidence confirms that antibiotic use and environmental factors accelerate the selection and spread of resistance genes, including the evolution of resistance to novel antimicrobial peptides.

item.title: Is your social media making you feel alone?
item.description: Active social media use is linked to greater online support. While problematic use correlates with loneliness, active engagement is linked to better wellbeing and support. The evidence shows that while problematic and addictive social media use correlates with loneliness and distress, active engagement can be linked to positive outcomes like online support.

item.title: Does wealth always lead to dishonesty?
item.description: Governance structure determines the flow of corruption. Corruption is not a constant in autocratic systems. It depends on whether the government is consolidated or lenient., The evidence shows that corruption is complex and varies depending on the specific structure of autocratic governance and the perception of property by rulers.

item.title: Does wealth change your biology?
item.description: High income does not biologically prime you for risk. The evidence is mixed and does not provide a direct link to biological priming for risk-taking. High socioeconomic status is linked to specific neural responses regarding reputation. The evidence shows that socioeconomic status influences specific psychological motivations like reputation, but it does not provide a direct link to biological priming for risk-taking.

item.title: Is your job physically changing your brain?
item.description: Corporate hierarchy does not reshape your brain. There is no evidence that your position in a company physically alters your neural pathways. Research focuses on behavior and burnout, not brain structure. The sources show that empathy is a valuable leadership trait and can be influenced by interventions, but they do not provide any data on neural pathway changes.

item.title: Why do you choose pain over silence?
item.description: You may choose pain over silence. Some people choose to administer strong electric shocks to themselves even when a mild or no-shock option is available. The evidence is mixed, showing that while some individuals avoid solitude through self-inflicted pain, other studies suggest thinking is generally pleasant and that pain-seeking behavior may be driven by curiosity.

item.title: Is your personality being rewritten by an algorithm?
item.description: The evidence does not show algorithms reshape your personality. While algorithms can reproduce biases from training data, there is no current evidence linking them to the active reshaping of long-term personality traits. The evidence shows that personality is dynamic and can be influenced by choice architecture and external situations, but it does not link these specific mechanisms to the active reshaping of personality by social media algorithms.

item.title: Are you choosing your interests, or are they being curated for you?
item.description: Algorithms structure what you see but may not change what you believe. Evidence shows recommender systems limit viewpoint diversity and structure information exposure. However, the evidence for direct ideological polarization is limited and may be driven by human cognitive mechanisms. The sources confirm that algorithms create environments with less diversity, but they also show that these effects are complex, potentially influenced by human psychology rather than just the technology.

item.title: Is your deep focus actually a malfunction?
item.description: Hyperfocus is linked to addictive behaviors. Evidence connects hyperfocus to malfunctions in attentional control, specifically in people with ADHD. This link is observed in both addictive behaviors and exercise addiction. The evidence shows that hyperfocus is associated with ADHD traits, addictive behaviors, and exercise addiction, but it does not establish a causal link to evolutionary survival or specific neurotransmitter-driven 'flow' states.

item.title: Is remote work changing how you relate to others?
item.description: Remote settings remove non-verbal clues from communication. When face-to-face interaction decreases, the cues you rely on for connection are often absent. The evidence shows that remote and online environments can disrupt social connections and remove non-verbal cues, but it does not provide data on specific levels of emotional intelligence.

item.title: Do you choose your next move?
item.description: Neural activity precedes your decision to move. The readiness potential is a slow buildup of electrical potential associated with movement preparation. It occurs before you report making a choice. The evidence shows that the readiness potential is associated with movement preparation but is not a causal driver of conscious intention.

item.title: When does your freedom feel like a burden?
item.description: Choice overload is not a universal rule. A meta-analysis of 63 conditions found a mean effect size of virtually zero for choice overload. The evidence shows that while choice overload can occur under specific conditions, it is not a consistent effect and can sometimes be mitigated or even reversed by factors like diversification.

item.title: Can you trust the details of your past?
item.description: The process that helps you make connections also creates false memories. The same cognitive mechanism used to make successful inferences contributes to the misattribution of reward-context in memory. The evidence shows that the same cognitive processes used to link different memories to make new connections also contribute to the creation of false memories and distorted contexts.

item.title: Who is actually deciding if you are qualified?
item.description: Technical limitations are not being put into practice. There is a disconnect between the documentation of AI risks and the governance frameworks meant to manage them. The evidence confirms that AI-recruitment systems can replicate human biases and suffer from design-related flaws, but it highlights a gap between identifying these risks and operationalizing technical solutions.

item.title: Did technology choose your life?
item.description: Technology is not an independent force. The evidence shows a complex tension between technological determinism and the active roles of human leadership and societal needs. The evidence shows a complex tension between technological determinism as a historical driver and the active roles of human leadership, societal needs, and specific actor-driven trajectories.

item.title: Was that your choice, or their design?
item.description: Digital interfaces transform reflective decisions into impulsive acts. Design mechanisms in digital credit and e-commerce exploit cognitive biases to drive behavior. These patterns replace deliberation with immediate action. The evidence shows that specific digital interface designs exploit psychological biases to drive impulsive behaviors and overconsumption.

item.title: Does your phone make you blind to your surroundings?
item.description: There is no data on physical hazards. The current evidence does not show how smartphone use affects your ability to see physical dangers. The provided sources do not contain data regarding the impact of smartphone use on the perception of physical hazards.

item.title: Why do you trust the people you see?
item.description: Bias does not always dictate your trust. While implicit biases influence many social interactions, some patient dissatisfaction is independent of those biases. The evidence shows that implicit biases significantly shape social and economic trust and influence healthcare interactions, but they do not always account for all patient perceptions.

item.title: Who owns the data from your routine?
item.description: Predictive systems turn group data into individual predictions. Statistical inferences about a group are transformed into specific predictions about you. The sources show that large corporations use behavioral surplus and predictive analytics to create systems of certainty and extraction across various industries.

item.title: Does switching tasks actually drain your brain?
item.description: Switching tasks can trigger neural disengagement. In specific contexts, moving between tasks is linked to reduced neural activity in brain regions responsible for processing. The sources show that prefrontal cortex volume relates to executive function and that switching can lead to neural disengagement, but they do not directly measure how rapid task-switching degrades the prefrontal cortex's efficiency in a general multitasking context.

item.title: Is automation actually destroying the middle class?
item.description: Labor polarization disappears when only native workers are considered. The shift toward high- and low-skill jobs is significantly influenced by low-skilled immigration rather than just technological change. The evidence shows that while routine tasks are being automated and middle-skill jobs are declining in some contexts, the broader labor market polarization is complex and influenced by migration and regional differences.

item.title: Is your personality a biological byproduct?
item.description: Your microbiome predicts your personality traits. Specific bacterial genera in your gut are significantly predicted by your personality traits. This link is supported by research but is not yet proven as a direct cause. The evidence shows a measurable link between gut microbiome composition and behavioral traits like personality and temperament, but it does not definitively prove that the microbiome is the primary cause of personality.

item.title: Is your phone revealing a hidden cognitive weakness?
item.description: Digital stimuli may unmask underlying cognitive vulnerabilities. Repeated engagement with task-irrelevant digital stimuli is linked to cortico-striatal strengthening and prefrontal-parietal under-consolidation. The evidence on whether this prevents the brain from entering the default mode network state for creativity is mixed. The sources confirm that digital distractions can create a self-reinforcing cycle of fragmented attention and reduced engagement, but they do not provide direct evidence that this specifically prevents the brain from entering the default mode network state for creativity.

item.title: Can you trust your own memories?
item.description: You can remember things that never happened. Misinformation can implant rich autobiographical false memories. This effect is stronger when guided imagery or pressure to answer is used. The evidence shows that false memories can be successfully implanted or distorted by misinformation, though the extent of this effect varies by individual cognitive traits and the specific methods used.

item.title: Does your phone actually make you feel closer?
item.description: Digital tools can foster closeness and self-esteem. Evidence suggests that digital communication can enhance self-esteem and foster closeness rather than simply reducing the rewards of face-to-face interaction. These findings are mixed or contested as there is no data on the neurological rewards of deep face-to-face interaction. The evidence suggests that digital communication can actually enhance self-esteem and foster closeness rather than simply reducing the rewards of face-to-face interaction.

item.title: Why do you believe what you see most often?
item.description: Exposure to longer misinformation creates a stronger belief in its truth. The longer you are exposed to a false statement, the more likely you are to accept it as fact. This effect happens regardless of your cognitive ability or thinking style. The evidence confirms that familiarity with information increases its perceived truthfulness, particularly when the exposure is prolonged.

item.title: Does vitamin D actually protect your bones?
item.description: Vitamin D does not prevent fractures in all healthy adults. Evidence shows benefits are highly specific to the condition, dosage, and individual genetics. The data is mixed and lacks sufficient evidence for broad health outcomes. The evidence shows that vitamin D's effects are highly specific to the condition, the dosage, and the individual's genetics rather than providing a universal benefit for all adults.

item.title: What does your biology say about colonial borders?
item.description: Colonialism left a genetic mark on southern African mammals. The two southernmost populations of cape buffalo have significantly lower heterozygosity levels of 0.33% and 0.29% compared to the rest of the population. The evidence regarding how arbitrary borders specifically shaped national genetic landscapes is mixed or contested. The evidence shows that colonial-era human impacts caused specific genetic diversity losses in southern African mammals and are detectable in human admixture history, but it does not provide a broad analysis of national border effects.

item.title: Who is directing your attention?
item.description: Algorithms are linked to increased polarization and impulsive buying. Studies show that personalized rankings and recommendation algorithms are linked to ideological extremism, emotional arousal, and impulsive purchasing.,,, The sources show that specific algorithmic designs and personalization features are linked to increased polarization and emotional arousal, but they also suggest potential ways to reduce these effects.

item.title: Does your card make you spend more?
item.description: The cashless effect is not a constant. The impact of card payments on spending varies depending on the economic cycle and the type of goods you purchase. The evidence confirms a significant but declining cashless effect that depends heavily on the context of the purchase.

item.title: Is your biology out of sync with your life?
item.description: Industrialisation created a biological mismatch for humans. Your biology is adapted for nature, but you live in an industrial world. This shift may have compromised human fitness. The sources suggest that industrialisation has created a biological and environmental mismatch for humans, but they do not provide specific evidence that it fundamentally rewired attention spans or neural processing.

item.title: Did war create the modern nation-state?
item.description: Warfare is linked to state formation, not the sole cause. The transition from empires to nation-states is not a simple result of war. Evidence shows a link, but the cause-and-effect is not settled. The evidence shows that state formation is linked to military competition and institutional innovation, but also involves complex religious and nationalistic factors.

item.title: Do you need to be similar to be happy?
item.description: Similarity is not a universal predictor of satisfaction. Some studies show personality similarity is unrelated to satisfaction, while others find it is positively associated. The evidence is inconsistent, showing that similarity is not a universal predictor of satisfaction and may instead be a byproduct of satisfaction.

item.title: Does the heat actually make you less smart?
item.description: Heat impairs complex learning more than simple tasks. While your brain handles basic reading well in the heat, complex tasks like mathematics suffer more. This evidence is mixed due to differences in study populations. The evidence shows that heat impacts complex learning more than simple tasks, but performance is not uniformly degraded across all temperatures.

item.title: Are you really only using half of your brain?
item.description: There is no global left-brained or right-brained phenotype. Data do not support a whole-brain phenotype of greater strength in one hemisphere over another across individuals. The evidence shows that while specific tasks and conditions (like handedness or neurodevelopmental disorders) influence hemispheric asymmetry, there is no evidence for a whole-brain phenotype of greater left or right-brain strength.
